summary: Introduces DECoupled Application Data Enroute (DECADE), a system letting content distribution applications such as peer-to-peer use in-network storage, to use network resources more efficiently. This document introduces the idea and its architecture.

eli5.summary: Like leaving packages in lockers around town so friends pick up nearby instead of far away.

subtitle: In-network storage for peer-to-peer and content distribution applications

tldr.problem: Content distribution applications like peer-to-peer (P2P) and streaming often use network resources inefficiently, requiring excessive bandwidth on last-mile links and backbone networks, creating bottlenecks that force operators to over-provision infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: DECADE introduces in-network storage servers where applications can store and retrieve data, allowing peers to fetch content from nearby storage instead of from distant peers or servers. Applications explicitly control what data is stored, who can access it, and when it expires, using token-based authorization.
tldr.outcome: By storing content inside the network closer to users, P2P and streaming applications can reduce overall bandwidth usage, improve user experience through lower latency, and ease capacity planning for network operators.

facts.label: Core protocols needed
facts.value: DRP (Data Resource Protocol), SDT (Standard Data Transfer)

today: RFC 7069 is an Informational document that remains active. The DECADE concepts and architecture continue to influence in-network storage and content distribution research. While a complete DECADE protocol specification was never standardized through IETF, the principles outlined—decoupling control and data planes, immutable object storage, explicit application control, token-based authorization—have been adopted in various forms by content delivery networks, peer-to-peer systems, and edge computing platforms. The document serves as a valuable reference for anyone designing distributed storage systems for content distribution applications.

sections.title: The Problem and DECADE Solution
sections.content:
Content distribution applications, especially peer-to-peer (P2P) systems and video streaming, dominate Internet traffic but often consume bandwidth inefficiently. In a traditional P2P network, peers fetch content from other distant peers, causing packets to traverse expensive backbone and last-mile links multiple times as different peers request the same content. Network operators must upgrade infrastructure to accommodate this traffic pattern, which is particularly expensive in the last mile—the connection from the network operator's core to individual homes and businesses. Upgrading the core infrastructure is cheaper, but it does not solve the fundamental problem of inefficient routing.

DECADE (DECoupled Application Data Enroute) addresses this by allowing applications to store data inside the network, at servers deployed by network operators or storage providers. Instead of fetching content from distant peers, an application endpoint can request data from a nearby DECADE server, reducing path length and bandwidth consumption. The key architectural principle is that applications retain explicit control: they decide what data to store, where to store it, who can access it, and when it should be deleted. This allows diverse content distribution applications (P2P, streaming, CDN hybrids) to adapt DECADE to their specific needs.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone going to one library far away, the town puts copies of popular books in small libraries nearby. The main library still controls which books go where and who can borrow them.

sections.title: Architectural Principles and System Components
sections.content:
DECADE is built on five core architectural principles. First, it decouples the data plane (actual data transfer) from the control plane (application logic like piece selection and overlay topology). This allows DECADE servers to be application-agnostic, supporting diverse content distribution models without encoding application-specific knowledge. Second, DECADE treats data as immutable—once stored, content is not modified, only deleted, which simplifies consistency and enables reuse. Third, data object identifiers (typically content hashes) are created by applications, allowing flexible naming schemes suitable to different applications. Fourth, applications have explicit control over resource allocation, access policies, and data placement rather than relying on automatic caching. Fifth, authorization uses delegation: applications generate tokens authorizing other applications to access data, avoiding the need for centralized access control lists.

A DECADE system consists of DECADE clients (integrated into applications) and DECADE servers (deployed in-network). The DECADE Resource Protocol (DRP) allows clients to configure access control and resource policies on servers, while the Standard Data Transfer protocol (SDT) handles actual data upload and download. Between these, applications implement their own control plane logic—search, indexing, piece selection, and overlay construction. DECADE servers may have dedicated data scheduling and resource controllers to manage bandwidth and storage fairly across multiple concurrent applications.
sections.eli5: The core library (server) just stores and retrieves data. Each town library (application endpoint) decides what to store and who gets access using permission tokens. This way different libraries can use the shared storage however they want.

sections.title: Protocol Considerations and Resource Management
sections.content:
DECADE is not itself a protocol but a system architecture for which specific protocols must be designed. The RFC recommends using RFC 6920 (Naming Things with Hashes) as the default naming scheme for data objects, allowing cryptographic verification that received data matches the requested name. For resource control, DECADE proposes a token-based system: when an application wishes to store data, it obtains a token from a DECADE server that can be passed to other applications, authorizing them to read specific data or use specific resources. Tokens include information about permitted operations, resource limits (bandwidth, storage size), and validity periods. This avoids the complexity of managing access control lists per object while still providing fine-grained control.

DECADE servers should manage two key resources: communication resources (upload and download bandwidth, number of simultaneous connections) and storage resources (total disk space, data retention time). Servers should support status queries allowing clients to learn what data is stored, how much resource capacity remains, and access statistics. The RFC suggests but does not mandate HTTP, CDMI (Cloud Data Management Interface), and OAuth as potential candidates for implementing DRP and SDT, recognizing that different deployments may have different requirements and existing infrastructure choices.
sections.eli5: Apps use permission tokens like library cards: 'I (app A) say app B can read this book for the next hour.' The library doesn't need to manage a big list of who owns what.

sections.title: Data Sequencing, Naming, and Attributes
sections.content:
DECADE data objects are immutable sequences of bytes identified by names chosen by applications. The naming scheme itself is application-agnostic—applications can name objects however they wish, whether based on content hashes (for file sharing), enumeration (for chunked downloads), time offsets (for video streaming), or custom schemes. A DECADE server simply stores and retrieves the bytes without enforcing any particular naming or sequencing semantics. This flexibility allows applications like live video streaming to break streams into variable-sized chunks and applications like file sharing to group multiple small chunks into larger objects without DECADE imposing a single model.

DECADE data objects can have associated attributes managed by the server, including expiration time (when the object can be deleted), media type (for content labeling), and access statistics (how often accessed, by which tokens). Applications can query and set these attributes based on their authorization level. Applications themselves handle higher-level metadata (like descriptions or playback information) either by embedding it inside data objects or through their own control plane mechanisms. This separation keeps DECADE servers simple while allowing applications to encode whatever metadata they need.
sections.eli5: The library stores blobs of bytes with expiration dates and access counters. Apps decide whether a blob is a movie, a song, or a document by how they use it.

sections.title: Security Model and Considerations
sections.content:
DECADE addresses three main security threats. First, denial-of-service attacks could overwhelm servers if many clients upload huge amounts of data or request massive replication. The RFC addresses this through authorization and resource control: servers only grant resources to authorized applications (via user delegation from the storage provider), and applications can delegate only limited resources to other applications via tokens with constraints on data size, bandwidth, and time. Second, compromised authorization mechanisms could allow unauthorized access. Token-based authorization depends on the strength of token generation and distribution—tokens must be kept confidential, should have limited validity periods, and should be signed to prevent forgery. Third, data spoofing could occur if an attacker injects fake data into the network or a compromised server. DECADE addresses this through name-object binding validation: applications verify that received data matches its name (typically via cryptographic hash), and they should not rely on servers to perform this validation.

The RFC emphasizes that DECADE does not enforce authentication of users (applications need not prove their identity to download data if they have a valid token), shifting security responsibility to applications. This enables anonymous access while maintaining fine-grained authorization control. Applications must use secure transport (like TLS/HTTPS) to protect token confidentiality, and they should validate received data to ensure it matches the requested name-object binding, especially in untrusted environments.
sections.eli5: Libraries prevent hoarding by limiting how much one person can store. They require valid tokens to prevent random people from adding books. Readers should verify a book is really what the title says.

sections.title: Deployment Models and Future Protocol Development
sections.content:
DECADE is designed to work in diverse deployment scenarios. ISPs might deploy DECADE servers at network borders or data centers to serve all subscribers, allocating each subscriber a quota of storage and bandwidth. Content distribution networks (CDNs) might use DECADE to coordinate content placement across their servers. Enterprise networks could use DECADE for internal peer-to-peer file sharing and video collaboration. Third-party storage providers might operate DECADE servers accessible to multiple ISPs and applications. The token-based delegation model supports all these scenarios: in ISP deployment, the ISP is the storage provider and issues user delegations to subscribers; in CDN deployment, the CDN is the provider; applications always control token generation for their own data.

The RFC emphasizes that DECADE is an architecture and set of principles, not a complete protocol specification. Future work must define specific DRP and SDT protocols, specifying exactly how applications request resource allocation, how tokens are formatted and validated, how data is named and located, and how servers exchange data with each other. The current document provides guidelines and evaluation of existing protocols (HTTP, CDMI, OAuth) as potential building blocks, allowing protocol designers to choose or combine existing standards rather than inventing wholly new protocols.
sections.eli5: Different places (ISPs, tech companies, offices) can run DECADE servers however they want, as long as they follow the general rules about tokens and storage. Future specs will detail exactly how servers talk to each other.
